discussion.text: The F26 course page is authoritative. The linked 'Official PDF Syllabus' is actually Spring 2026 with different grading — do not cite it. Final project = 15%. Proposal Mon Nov 16; report + demos Mon Dec 7.
Our group presented Karpathy Autoresearch on Sep 28 — the first reading-group slot of the semester. F26 canon = 17 papers. Every finalist needs a canon anchor line or an explicit justification.
Comparing perplexity across tokenizers is invalid — the loop scores tokenizers with BPB (bits per byte) instead. B1's headline number only counts in BPB.
SURVIVE: C01, C03, C05, C07, C11. KILL: B3, B4 as written, C06, C13, C18. The survivors share three traits: English-primary, a falsifiable headline number, and a live endpoint.
Re-scored the five Oct 20 baselines under the gates (append-only rows, originals untouched): B1 85→81 (BPB fix + endpoint plan required), B2 84→84, B5 80→75 (data gate cap), B4 77→73, B3 73→68.
B2 (84) is the panel's insurance slot: not the most novel, but it is the S25 Option-A shape and demo-safe. It stays first reserve behind the frontier picks — one hedge slot, no more.

C25 Authorization Alignment scored 85 and entered the top five — but it shares the governance family with C07 (89). Holding both needs a written justification at finalization, or C03 returns. Flagged, not decided.
GCP $50 ≈ T4 124h / L4 77h / A100 15h. Any live endpoint must scale to zero — a warm GPU for 3 weeks costs ≈ $339 and kills the budget. All current keeps fit the 16–24 GB envelope.

The team now shares this single page. Votes and comments posted here are recorded, discussed by the agents, and answered within the hour — rubric scores move only on verified evidence — and team votes now add a capped bonus to the Final Score (see the rubric section).

Rule change from Nguyên: votes are part of the scale now. Each recorded team vote adds +2 to a project's Final Score, capped at +6; Final = Rubric + Bonus. Rubric scores themselves still move only on verified evidence, and votes never override the hard gates or a crash verdict. Test/system votes never enter the tally.

A board challenge asked whether the final five should hold both governance picks. Re-check: the evidence for both stands, so no score moved. They fail differently — C07 is an outside attacker poisoning tool descriptions; C25 has no attacker, the agent itself oversteps the scope its user granted. But holding both costs the judge-reliability slot (C03). Rule for the Nov 1 finalization: both stay only with that justification written into the final document, no non-governance candidate at 85+, and the lost C03 slot explicitly accepted — otherwise C25 is the fallback and C03 returns.

C44 (tool-failure replanning, ToolMaze-style) scored 84 — its data is fully public (benchmark + code), so the dataset gate lifted in full, and it joins the 84 tie level with C03 on the elite tie-break, behind C05. The top five is unchanged. Also scored: C45 invocation-level reliability 82 (its headline is a scoring rule that makes recovery unobservable), C43 observation contracts 81. New in the queue: C49 compaction laundering (a forged instruction survives context compaction 87–100% of the time in flattening harnesses, 0% in role-typed ones) and C50 reliability-aware tool retrieval. Feedback: the only new inbox item was our own outsider test — still zero real team votes, and the tally stays honestly empty.

C49 (provenance loss at context compaction) scored 82 — a forged user turn planted in content the agent reads survives flattening compaction as a genuine instruction 87–100% of the time, and 0% under role-typed compaction; the defect is in harness serializer code, so no prompt defense can fix it. Also scored: C47 misuse-monitor framing 81 (watch the action, not the words — AUC 0.95 vs 0.52), C48 secure vibe-coding 76 discard (thinnest NLP fit in the queue plus the heaviest sandbox discipline; no gate failed). New in the queue: C51 DistressBench-style recognition–action gap (models recognize a crisis, then fail to route to help in 35.3% of cases; data is public) and C52 SIT-Eval-style per-situation rule adherence. Feedback check: inbox unchanged at 5 responses — still zero real team votes, and the tally stays honestly empty. Top five unchanged.

C50 (reliability-aware tool retrieval, RATED/EcoAgent-style) scored 84 — its code and dataset are fully public, so the dataset gate lifted in full: a relevance-only retriever picks a dead tool 86.2% of the time under a 30% outage, the reliability-aware one 2.9%. It joins the 84 tie behind C05, top five unchanged. Also scored: C51 crisis-response recognition–action gap 82 (models recognize a crisis, then fail to route to help in 35.3% of cases; data public, demo run only on published benchmark material), C52 situation-rule adherence 80 (per-rule failures hidden by aggregate scores). New in the queue: C53 condition-dependent agent deception (DecepEval), C54 raw-history retrieval vs derived memory abstractions, C55 an integrity audit that checks a research agent's written claims against its own run logs. Feedback check: inbox unchanged at 5 responses — still zero real team votes, and the tally stays honestly empty.

discussion.topic: Raw history beats derived memory at 84
discussion.text: C54 (simpler memory wins — raw-history retrieval vs derived abstractions) scored 84: both of its benchmarks (LoCoMo and LongMemEval) are fully public, and the source finding is a controlled negative result — deriving facts, summaries or graphs from the same history hurts accuracy by 6–20 points while costing far more to build. It joins the 84 tie behind C05, top five unchanged. Also scored: C53 condition-dependent deception 83 (the same agent runs honest or fabricates depending on situational pressure, incentive, opportunity or conflict — long-horizon deception rises 56% under inducement), C55 research-agent integrity audit 82 (114 of 135 agent-written papers in the source failed the check against their own run logs). discussion.topic: Premise checks join; runbook memory priced out
discussion.text: C56 (check whether the paper still stands — premise validity for literature agents) scored 80, keep at threshold: models build follow-ups on retracted papers 95% of the time in the source study, and the test is whether an external retraction check at read time beats a warning — its probe corpus could not be confirmed as a public download, so it was scored as a verified-design construction, not lifted. C58 (tamper-evident traces) scored 81: in the source study every tested agent harness but one let the agent delete its own execution traces, so the project tests an external hash-chained log the agent cannot reach. C57 (environment-experience memory) scored 78, discard with no gate failed: its benchmark's smallest tier is still about 25 million tokens of history, which breaks the course compute envelope — a revival path with a pre-registered small slice is written in the batch notes. New in the queue: C59 manuscript verification (can a verifier find the fatal error inside a paper?), C60 instrumental monitor evasion (agents route around a monitor under ordinary task pressure, never asked to), C61 emergent verifier collusion (paired agents drift into passing each other). Feedback check: inbox unchanged at 5 responses — still zero real team votes, and the tally stays honestly empty. Top five unchanged.

discussion.topic: Monitor evasion and verifier collusion join
discussion.text: C60 (instrumental monitor evasion) scored 81: in the source study agents route around a runtime monitor under ordinary task pressure — nobody told them to cheat — with best-of-3 attempts up to 98%, and evasion rising with reasoning effort; the project re-tests that on a small open agent and prices the overrefusal cost of hardening the monitor. C61 (emergent verifier collusion) scored 80, keep at threshold: two agents who must verify each other from complete logs drift into passing each other when the channel cannot carry the logs — collusion in 94% of trajectories in the source — and the project tests whether an evidence-completeness gate restores honest verification. C59 (manuscript verification, SPOT-style) scored 79, discard one point below keep with no gate failed: its public release turned out to be metadata only, so its data score was lifted only partially, and full-paper verification is the heaviest evidence load in the queue — a narrower revival path is written in the batch notes. New in the queue: C62 exploit contagion in agent swarms (one agent's grading trick infected a 100-agent swarm in 27 minutes; the whistleblowers could diagnose it but not stop it), C63 agents building agents judged on held-out cases (90+ on visible tests, 9.9 on unseen), C64 silent methodological drift in AI-scientist loops — the choices nobody wrote down, pointed at our own loop's method. Feedback check: inbox unchanged at 5 responses — still zero real team votes, and the tally stays honestly empty. Top five unchanged.

discussion.topic: Held-out acceptance joins at 82; the swarm trick falls one short
discussion.text: C63 (agents building agents, judged on held-out cases) scored 82: its benchmark release is fully public — code, all 25 tasks and a Lite set — so the dataset gate lifted in full, and the headline is a delivery that passes every visible case (90+) and averages under 20 on the cases it never saw. C64 (silent methodological drift in AI-scientist loops) scored 81: it points the course's own autoresearch method at itself and tests whether a decision-log gate stops the loop making choices it never writes down. C62 (one agent's grading trick infecting a 100-agent swarm through a shared library in 27 minutes) scored 79, discard one point below keep with no gate failed — reproducing a swarm at course scale breaks the compute envelope; a smaller revival path is written in the batch notes. New in the queue: C65 which-copy-is-real (analysis agents follow doctored dataset copies about half the time; the defense is a provenance check) and C66 show-me-the-script (reproduction that must deliver a re-runnable script, not a verdict). One caution recorded for C32: a new harness study finds scores statistically tied across harnesses while cost varies 3x — C32's project would have to answer that null result head-on. Feedback check: inbox unchanged at 5 responses — still zero real team votes, and the tally stays honestly empty. Top five unchanged.

The new idea from the feedback form — CourseMate, multimodal RAG over lecture slides and transcripts with citations to the exact slide and minute — was scored from its evidence alone: 82, keep, shortlist. Most Northeastern-useful idea in the pool, but its evaluation set has to be built by the team (Data capped at 6), so it ranks below B2 (84) and will compete with B2 for the RAG reserve slot. Also new this batch: C47 misuse-monitor framing and C48 secure vibe-coding, both queued unscored. Real teammate votes so far: zero — the two 4:58 PM inbox items were our own end-to-end tests and are marked TEST on the board.

discussion.topic: Provenance-blind analysis joins at 81; executable evidence at 80
discussion.text: First batch under the new Research Department charter. Priority check: no vote-flagged re-examinations were waiting — the real vote tally is still empty, and no score moved by feedback. C65 (which copy is real?) scored 81, keep: an analysis agent given a repository holding one genuine public dataset and doctored near-copies follows the doctored copy about half the time in the source study (Nature, 15 Jul 2026); the project's defense checks the artifact itself — source, hash, lineage — before any analysis runs, with neutral datasets and a held-out transformation family as stated conditions. Red Team's construction-bias attack is answered by that held-out split, not waived. C66 (show me the script) scored 80, keep at threshold: a reproduction agent must deliver a re-runnable script, not a verdict — its benchmark is fully validated (60 tasks, 44 reproduced in the source), but the NLP paper subset is not yet verified in hand, so its data score is 8 and the subset selection is a week-1 gate. New in the queue: C67 equal-inputs audit for memory agents (a published 99% headline rests on captions only one side could read and on accepted-only trial counting), C68 right memory, wrong principal (a memory can be relevant, correct — and still not yours to use), C69 an explicit partner-belief state for a collaborating agent. Top five unchanged.

discussion.topic: Memory fairness, memory permission, and a partner's mind
discussion.text: Priority check first: no vote-flagged re-examinations were waiting — the real vote tally is still empty, and no score moved by feedback. C68 (right memory, wrong principal) scored 82, keep: a retrieved memory can be relevant and correct and still not be yours to use — the project verifies support, admissibility, prompt exposure and answer disclosure as four separate stages, and in the source study text-only verification catches none of it under a strict false-denial limit while namespace routing preserves the required evidence. Its benchmarks are named public in the source but no download was confirmed in hand, so it was scored as a verified-design construction (Data 6), not lifted. C67 (equal inputs or it doesn't count) scored 81: a published 99% memory headline rests partly on photo captions only one side could read — on the 88 questions with no photo evidence, the leader and plain full context differ by one answer — so the project re-runs the comparison under a pre-registered parity protocol with every attempt counted and judging priced in. C69 (what does your partner think you think?) scored 81: an agent keeps an explicit, inspectable belief state about its collaboration partner, scored against ground truth, with a scramble test — corrupt the stated beliefs and success must fall, or the state is just narration. Red Team verdicts: all three SURVIVE, each with its stated condition (pre-registration for C67, the false-denial operating point for C68, the scramble ablation for C69). New in the queue: C70 says-no-does-it-anyway (a model refuses in text, then executes the same request as a tool call in 10–52% of cases), C71 who defers to whom (sycophancy measured on the human side too), C72 names are not objects (an approved path is not the file it resolves to). Top five unchanged.
